title: Reading practice: Building the Transcontinental Railroad and Two Letters About City Spending
description: Eight reading items about a short history of the transcontinental railroad and two letters that argue for different uses of city money, practicing explaining effects, sequencing events and judging arguments.

stimuli.title: Building the Transcontinental Railroad
paragraphs: In the 1860s, the United States stretched from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean, but traveling from one coast to the other was slow and dangerous. Travelers crossed the plains and mountains in wagons, or they sailed around South America, and either trip could take several months. As a result, moving people and goods to the West was slow and very expensive.

To solve this problem, Congress passed a law in 1862 that supported building a railroad across the country: the transcontinental railroad. Two companies shared the job. The Central Pacific built eastward from California, and the Union Pacific built westward from Nebraska. Many people doubted that the two lines could ever meet, because the route crossed deserts and the high Sierra Nevada mountains. Nevertheless, work began in 1863.

Building the railroad was an enormous task. Together, the two lines stretched nearly 1,800 miles and were built mostly by hand. Workers, including thousands of immigrants from China and Ireland, used picks, shovels, and explosives to level the ground and to cut tunnels through rock. The two lines finally met at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869.

The results were dramatic. A trip across the country that once took months could now be made by train in about a week. Because travel became faster and cheaper, more settlers moved west, farmers and ranchers could ship their products to eastern cities, and new towns grew along the tracks. In addition, goods from the West Coast could reach the East quickly.

Not everyone benefited equally, however. Construction was dangerous, and many workers faced hard labor, harsh winters, and low pay. Later, cars, highways, and airplanes offered even faster travel, and fewer people traveled by train.

stimuli.title: Letters to the Editor: How Should Millbrook Spend Its Extra Money?
paragraphs: Millbrook’s city council has about two million dollars left over from last year’s budget. The council can use the money for only one major project: extending the bus routes to the east side of town, or repairing and expanding the public library. Two residents explain their positions in letters to the local newspaper.

Rafael Torres writes that the bus extension should come first. In his view, many families on the east side have no car, so workers cannot easily reach jobs on the other side of town. He points out that a city survey found that about one in four east-side workers spends more than an hour traveling each way. Torres also argues that more riders would mean fewer cars on crowded roads. Although a library is valuable, he says, a person without transportation cannot even reach it.

Mai Nguyen disagrees. She argues that the library should receive the money because it serves people of every age, not only workers. According to her letter, the library’s computers are used by students and job seekers every day, and its roof leaks so badly that the children’s section was closed last winter. Nguyen admits that buses matter, but she believes that the city can pay for bus routes with other funds, such as ticket sales and state grants, while a repaired library has no other source of money.
Both writers want to help residents, but they disagree about which need is more urgent. Readers must decide whose evidence is stronger.

items.stem: According to the passage, why did more settlers move west after the railroad was finished?

options.text: Travel across the country became faster and cheaper than it was before.
The government paid the cost of every ticket for settlers who went west.
The railroad companies ordered people to move west to fill the new towns.
Highways and airplanes made long trips quicker for every traveler.

distractors.b: The passage never says that the government paid for tickets. It says travel became cheaper.
distractors.c: The passage never says the companies ordered anyone to move. It says settlers moved west because travel was faster and cheaper.
distractors.d: Highways and airplanes came later, as paragraph 5 says. They did not cause settlers to move west at first.

items.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that because travel became faster and cheaper, more settlers moved west.

support.clue: Go to paragraph 4. Find the sentence that begins with “Because” and read the cause it gives.
support.model: Mentor example (a different cause). “Fruit became cheaper in the town because a new road let trucks reach the farms directly.” The word “because” introduces the reason for the change. Find the reason that settlers moved west.

misconceptions.c: invents an order from the companies

facts: The transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869 and cut the trip across the United States from months by wagon or ship to about a week by train.
Highways and airplanes came after the railroad and offered even faster travel.

items.stem: Put these events from the history of the railroad in the order they happened.

items.text: The two lines met in Utah in 1869.
Trips to the West took months, so travel was slow and costly.
Later, cars, highways, and airplanes offered even faster travel.
Congress passed a law in 1862 that supported a railroad across the country.
Many people doubted the plan, but work began in 1863.

items.explanation: The slow travel problem came first, then the law in 1862, then the start of work in 1863, the meeting of the two lines in 1869, and later the cars and airplanes.

support.clue: Look for dates and time words: In the 1860s, 1862, work began in 1863, 1869, and Later.
support.model: Mentor example (a different history). “In the 1950s, a town had only one bridge. Next, citizens proposed a second bridge. In 1962, builders finished it. Later, traffic grew.” Dates and time words show the order of events. Use the dates in the railroad passage to order its events.

facts: Congress passed the Pacific Railway Act in 1862; work on the transcontinental railroad began in 1863 and the two lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869.
Cars, highways and airplanes came later and offered faster travel.

items.stem: Choose the phrases that best complete the explanation of the railroad’s purpose, its difficulty, and its effects.

dropdown.template: Congress passed a law in 1862 in order to {1}. Building the railroad was difficult because {2}. As a result of the finished railroad, {3}.

options: support a railroad across the country
stop wagons from crossing the plains
1.answer: support a railroad across the country

options: the route crossed deserts and high mountains
the two companies refused to share the work
workers were not allowed to use tools
2.answer: the route crossed deserts and high mountains

options: more settlers moved west and new towns grew along the tracks
the trip across the country took longer than before
farmers and ranchers could no longer ship their products
3.answer: more settlers moved west and new towns grew along the tracks

items.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives the purpose of the 1862 law (support a railroad across the country) and the difficulty (deserts and the high Sierra Nevada mountains). Paragraph 4 gives the result: more settlers moved west and new towns grew.

support.clue: Use paragraphs 2 through 4. Blank 1 is a purpose, blank 2 is a difficulty, and blank 3 is a result.
support.frame: The law was passed in order to ______. The work was hard because ______. As a result, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different project). “The village built a well to supply clean water. Digging was hard because the ground was rocky. As a result, families no longer carried water from the river.” Look for a purpose, a difficulty, and a result. Find each one in the railroad passage.

facts: The Central Pacific and Union Pacific built the transcontinental railroad from opposite ends, and it crossed deserts and the Sierra Nevada mountains.
Settlers moved west and towns grew along the railroad after it opened.

items.stem: Which TWO details in paragraph 5 show that building the railroad had costs for workers?

options.text: Farmers and ranchers could ship goods to eastern cities.
Many workers received low pay for their hard labor.
Highways and airplanes later offered even faster travel.
The work of building the railroad was dangerous for workers.

distractors.a: This is a benefit of the railroad, and it appears in paragraph 4. It is not a cost to workers.
distractors.c: Highways and airplanes are mentioned as later competition for the railroad. They are not a cost that the workers faced.

items.explanation: Paragraph 5 says construction was dangerous and that many workers faced hard labor, harsh winters, and low pay.

support.clue: Reread paragraph 5. The word “however” signals a contrast with the benefits in paragraph 4. Then ask who is affected by each detail.
support.frame: One cost to workers was ______. Another cost was ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different situation). “The new stadium brought visitors to the town. However, nearby families dealt with noise and traffic.” The word “however” introduces the costs after the benefits. Find the costs that follow “however” in the railroad passage.

misconceptions.c: picks a true detail that answers a different question

facts: Building the transcontinental railroad was dangerous, and many workers faced hard labor, harsh winters and low pay.

items.stem: Which TWO facts about the council’s decision does the text state?

options.text: The council has already voted to repair the public library.
The council has about two million dollars left over from last year.
The council plans to build a new park near the river.
The council can use the money for only one major project.

distractors.a: The text says the council has not decided. The two letters argue about the choice.
distractors.c: A park is not mentioned. The choices are the bus routes and the library.

items.explanation: The first paragraph states the amount of money and says it can be used for only one major project.

support.clue: Read the first paragraph. Look for the amount of money and the limit on how it can be used.
support.frame: The council has ______ to spend, and it can fund ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different decision). “The club has fifty dollars and can buy only one game: a board game or a puzzle.” The first sentence states the amount and the limit. Look for the amount and the limit in the first paragraph of the letters.

misconceptions.a: assumes the decision is already made
misconceptions.c: adds a detail that is not in the text

facts: The scenario about Millbrook is fictional.

items.stem: Match each description of a writer’s argument to the sentence that fits it.

right.text: The library’s roof leaks so badly that the children’s section was closed last winter.
Buses matter, but bus routes can be paid for with other funds.
A city survey found that about one in four east-side workers spends more than an hour traveling each way.
A library is valuable, but a person without transportation cannot even reach it.

items.explanation: Evidence is a fact or example, such as the survey or the closed children’s section. An admitted point agrees that the other side has value (“Although a library is valuable”, “Nguyen admits that buses matter”) before the writer argues back.

support.clue: Evidence is a fact or example. An admitted point says the other side has some value; look for words such as Although and admits.
support.frame: He admits that ______, but he argues that ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different argument). “Although the pool is expensive to run, it gives every child a safe place to swim.” The first part admits a point, and the second part is the writer’s main argument. Use the same idea to match each writer’s admitted point and evidence.

facts: The Millbrook letters are a fictional scenario.

items.stem: Sort each statement from the letters: is it a claim or evidence?

tokens.text: The bus extension should come first.
The library should receive the money.
The library’s roof leaks, and the children’s section was closed last winter.
A city survey found that about one in four east-side workers travels more than an hour each way.
Many east-side families have no car.

items.explanation: A claim says what the council should do. Evidence gives facts the writer uses to persuade: the leaking roof, the survey, and the families without cars.

support.clue: Ask: is this what the writer wants the council to do, or a fact the writer uses to persuade?
support.frame: A claim tells what ______. Evidence gives ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different argument). Claim: “Our class should adopt a classroom plant.” Evidence: “Plants make the room look welcoming, and our school allows small plants.” The claim is the goal, and the evidence is the support. Sort the letters’ statements the same way.

facts: The Millbrook letters are a fictional scenario.

items.stem: Which statement best describes how the two writers’ arguments are different?

options.text: Torres wants the city to save the money, but Nguyen wants the city to spend all of it now.
Torres says that libraries have no value, but Nguyen says that buses have no value.
Torres relies on facts and numbers, but Nguyen relies only on her own opinions about the library.
Torres stresses jobs and travel for workers, but Nguyen stresses services for people of every age.

distractors.a: Both writers want the council to spend the money. They disagree about which project should get it.
distractors.b: Both writers admit that the other project has value. They differ about which need is more urgent.
distractors.c: Nguyen gives evidence too: the leaking roof, the closed children’s section, and daily computer use.

items.explanation: Torres argues about workers who cannot reach jobs, while Nguyen argues that the library serves people of every age.

support.clue: Compare who each writer says the project will help most. Reread the first sentence of each writer’s paragraph and the reasons that follow.
support.model: Mentor example (a different comparison). “Mr. Lee argues that the park needs lights because safety matters most, while Ms. Abara argues that it needs benches because comfort for older visitors matters most.” Compare the writers by what each says matters most. Do the same with the two letters.

facts: The Millbrook letters are a fictional scenario.
